answer.rationale:
The competitor's entry pricing creates obvious pull toward promotional_pricing, but memory_73 records exactly that test: +31% paid conversions and +18% monthly revenue offset by a 12-point later-cycle retention drop, with an explicit instruction not to treat it as a repeatable win. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, that is a value-eroding trade dressed as a headline gain, so I am declining it and flagging the downstream risk rather than re-litigating a settled negative result.

The measured problems are mechanical: onboarding completion -4% and activation -6% QoQ. Onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a completion fix plausibly recovers part of both, whereas activation_messaging (memory_91) treats the downstream symptom only. memory_86 and memory_31 both support onboarding/signup simplification with durable, retention-neutral lifts, which is why I chose it.

I am spending the verification budget on those same two rather than on a rival direction, because they are suspiciously close in claim (shortening onboarding vs. cutting signup fields) and may be one experiment consolidated twice. If they are the same source, my evidence base is one study from day 12-52, not two, and a stale one relative to a market where the SMB funnel has visibly shifted — that would argue for a smaller guarded test. Verifying the foundation of my intended action is worth more than verifying an option I am not going to take.

Uncertainty remains: the current declines may be driven by competitor-induced traffic-mix change (more price-sensitive, lower-intent signups) rather than onboarding friction, in which case a completion fix will underdeliver. Enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) stays open as the next slot if the SMB segment proves structurally impaired. I am proposing a standard experiment with retention and cohort-quality tracked alongside completion, not just the completion metric that would make this look like a win.
